detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.name: MISO
sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.name: Southwest Power Pool
sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The EIA commercial-sector sales snapshot for June 2026 shows Texas with the largest volume among the eight listed states at 15,753.83 MWh and the lowest average price at 8.66, while California has the highest price at 27.33 with 10,024.68 MWh. Virginia, a major data center market, reports 7,770.67 MWh at an average price of 10.99. These commercial sales are a proxy for data center load, not a direct measurement, because data centers are mostly billed in the commercial class.

Across the five interconnection queues, planned generation and storage waiting to connect totals 438,086.5 MW in ERCOT, 319,115.45 MW in NYISO, 299,720.6 MW in MISO, 198,074.27 MW in SPP, and 71,608.82 MW in CAISO. These are not data center demand itself, but storage and gas additions in these queues are the categories most likely to track load growth from data centers. In ERCOT, storage leads at 159,820.34 MW and gas is 78,092.4 MW; in MISO, storage is 67,026.89 MW and gas 30,236.33 MW; in SPP, storage is 52,513.09 MW and gas 47,221.675 MW. CAISO storage is 46,870.26 MW with only 915.6 MW gas. NYISO's queue is unusual: 291,156.45 MW falls in the "other" category, with gas at 27,879 MW and solar at just 80 MW. These queues are not directly comparable because each operator counts projects differently; ERCOT includes large generators with a full interconnection study requested, NYISO publishes its queue as-is, MISO and SPP include all statuses, and CAISO counts active requests with completed and withdrawn projects separately.

For data center readers, the key signal is the large storage and gas capacity in ERCOT, MISO, and SPP, which suggests developers are positioning for flexible and dispatchable supply in markets with growing load. Solar remains the largest single category in ERCOT at 150,347.17 MW and in MISO at 146,004.28 MW, but storage is close behind in ERCOT and exceeds gas in MISO and SPP. The EIA price spread, from 8.66 in Texas to 27.33 in California, also matters for siting decisions. What to watch next is whether the large "other" category in NYISO and the storage-heavy queues in ERCOT and CAISO convert to actual in-service capacity over the next few quarterly updates.
